sources.title: Wikipedia GeoSearch, 2 km radius around Five Points, Downtown Atlanta
National Register of Historic Places listings in Fulton County, Georgia

stops.name: Georgia State Capitol
stops.description: Georgia has governed itself from this 1889 statehouse ever since, under a 75-foot dome crowned by the statue known as Miss Freedom.

stops.name: Central Presbyterian Church
stops.description: The 1885 sanctuary faces the Capitol straight across Washington Street, so the congregation and the legislature have stared at each other for well over a century.

stops.name: Shrine of the Immaculate Conception
stops.address: 48 Martin Luther King Jr Dr SW
stops.description: The wooden church that stood here was shelled during the Civil War and pressed into service as a hospital, then rolled aside in 1869 so this brick one could take its place.

stops.name: Atlanta City Hall
stops.description: City government has run out of this 1930 neo-Gothic tower for nearly a century, one block off the Capitol grounds.

stops.name: Fulton County Courthouse
stops.description: Built between 1911 and 1914, this is still where Fulton County hears its cases.

stops.name: Atlanta Constitution Building
stops.description: The Atlanta Constitution outgrew this plant and left in 1953; the building was added to the National Register in January 2026 and still carries Julian Harris's long bas-relief on the history of the press.

stops.name: Woodruff Park
stops.description: Downtown's central green, holding the Phoenix sculpture of a woman releasing the bird that stands for the city's rise from Sherman's ashes.

stops.name: Flatiron Building
stops.description: Finished in 1897, this wedge is the oldest skyscraper still standing in Atlanta and it beat New York's better-known Flatiron by five years.

stops.name: Candler Building
stops.description: Coca-Cola money built this 1906 tower for Asa Candler, whose Central Bank and Trust kept its headquarters inside.

stops.name: Hurt Building
stops.description: Seventeen floors begun in 1913, wrapped around a three-story domed rotunda whose original chandelier still hangs under gold-leaf sunbursts.

stops.name: Healey Building
stops.description: A 1913 Late Gothic Revival tower in Fairlie-Poplar, worth stepping inside for the daylit atrium behind the storefronts.

stops.name: Ellis Hotel
stops.description: This was the Winecoff, the hotel that burned in 1946 in the deadliest hotel fire in American history; it reopened in 1951 with the alarms and sprinklers it had never had.

stops.name: Big Bethel AME Church
stops.description: The anchor church of Sweet Auburn, where the Atlanta Negro Voters League held its annual meetings through the 1960s.

stops.name: APEX Museum
stops.description: Dan Moore founded this Auburn Avenue museum in 1978 to tell the city's and the country's history from a Black perspective.

stops.name: Centennial Olympic Park
stops.description: Laid out for the 1996 Summer Olympics and kept afterward, with the Fountain of Rings still spraying children on hot afternoons.

note: Atlanta had never been scouted; the log only had Boston, Buffalo, Charlotte, Chicago, Cincinnati and Cleveland, so Atlanta wins alphabetically among the never-run cities. All 15 stops sit inside a walkable loop from Five Points: the Capitol/City Hall block to the south, Peachtree and Fairlie-Poplar in the middle, Sweet Auburn about half a mile east, and Centennial Olympic Park about two-thirds of a mile northwest. Every stop has a verified street address; ZIPs were confirmed one by one against a map service, so none are missing. Dropped: the Atlanta Zero Mile Post, which reads like a perfect stop but was moved out of downtown to the Atlanta History Center in Buckhead in October 2018; Underground Atlanta, whose article gives no street address and which closed in 2016 with its current public access unclear; and the Statue of Henry W. Grady and the Five Points Monument, both real and both standing, but neither Wikipedia nor the NRHP rows give them a street address and I would not invent one. Held back only to keep the batch at 15, and worth adding if you want more Sweet Auburn: the Odd Fellows Building and Auditorium, 250 Auburn Ave NE, 30303 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odd_Fellows_Building_and_Auditorium). Note that the NRHP row for the Fulton County Courthouse says 160 Pryor St SW while the article body says 136 Pryor St SW; I used the article's number.
